title: Payroll 2.0
protagonist: Francesca Molianari, founder and owner of Grampoline LLC
primary_metric: dollars removed from the $25,000 remaining-2019-payroll shortfall target

options.A: Full Stop -- let one employee go, closing the $25,000 shortfall in a single cut
options.B: Even Keel -- cut every remaining employee's pay by the same percentage, closing the same $25,000 shortfall

overview_numerals_cleared.reason: Years since the storefront opened -- sensory/scene-setting texture in the Overview, never used in any calculation. The $25,000 target, all dollar figures, and every year are deliberately withheld from the Overview and stated only in Background/Appendices.

modeling_assumptions.text: Grampoline LLC's financial history (Appendix B) and per-employee payroll (Appendix C) are the original case materials' own dataset, carried forward from the source workbook -- Grampoline is fictional, not a real business, so these figures are not subject to external, real-world sourcing (see legacy_conversion_note).

The $25,000 shortfall target and Even Keel's percent-cut base are both computed over the five hired employees' H2-2019 projected pay (Appendix C), excluding Francesca's own remaining pay -- she has already gone a month without a paycheck (Background), and the Dilemma is about the team she built, not about herself.

Where a full-year 2019 figure is needed but only a first-half actual exists (D4), this case assumes second-half revenue and expenses continue at the same rate as the first half -- no seasonal pattern is given anywhere in the source data, so a flat continuation is the simplest assumption that does not invent a trend the case never states.

The Twist (FACILITATOR.md, facilitator-only) assumes Christina's stated 41% share of 2018 new sales (Appendix A) is representative of her share of 2017-to-2018 revenue growth specifically -- the case's own data gives a new-sales split, not a growth-by-salesperson breakdown, so this is a disclosed scenario assumption filling a real gap in the given data, not a sourced fact.

deliverables.text: A bar graph comparing each of Grampoline's five employees' projected remaining 2019 pay (Appendix C).

If your position is A (Full Stop): the name of the employee you let go, the exact dollar amount removed from the remaining payroll budget, and why that employee and not one of the other four -- grounded in whether their remaining pay actually closes the $25,000 target, not just in their story.

If your position is B (Even Keel): the flat percent pay cut, applied to all five employees, that removes exactly $25,000 from the remaining payroll budget -- shown employee by employee, with each person's new remaining-pay figure.

A projected end-of-2019 profit table for your chosen option, built by scaling Grampoline's first-half 2019 revenue and expenses (Appendix B) to a full year, combined with your option's adjusted second-half payroll (Appendix C).

A year-by-year trend graph of Grampoline's profit from 2011 through 2018 (Appendix B), with a trend line you draw from a linear equation you write from that data, extended to project profit for 2020 under your chosen option.

balance.argument_a: Only Christina's projected remaining 2019 pay ($26,450) is large enough on its own to close the $25,000 shortfall in a single cut -- every other employee falls short (Martha and Irene by $1,600 each, Paul by $4,500, Tiago by $6,500). Letting Christina go removes $26,450 from the books immediately and permanently, with zero dependency on getting a percentage exactly right, and leaves the other four employees with every dollar they were counting on.
balance.argument_b: A flat percent cut, applied to all five employees, closes the identical $25,000 gap without anyone losing their job or their income entirely. It spreads one real hardship across five households instead of concentrating all of it onto Christina and hers -- and it keeps Grampoline's single strongest driver of new sales (41% of 2018's new sales, more than double Paul's 17%, Appendix A) on the floor at the exact moment the company most needs revenue growing.
balance.margin_basis: Full Stop (via Christina, the only single-employee fit that actually closes the gap) removes $26,450 from the $25,000 target; Even Keel is constructed to remove exactly $25,000. Margin = (26450-25000)/25000 = 5.8%, computed on the primary metric (dollars removed from the shortfall target). See derived{} for the full worked figures.
balance.stability: Sensitivity to be confirmed by a full Tier 2 gate run (case.json.qa records the outcome once probe 5 executes). By construction: flexing the one genuine FLEX[] dial (christina_growth_attribution_pct, the Twist's disclosed 41%-of-new-sales-as-proxy-for-growth-share assumption) does not touch the base evaluate() comparison at all -- it only affects evaluate_twist(), and only on the Christina branch of Option A. At +/-50% (attribution 20.5% or 61.5%), the Twist's at-risk-revenue figure moves between $2,870 and $8,610, so Full Stop + Christina's net twisted benefit ranges from $17,840 to $23,580 -- in every case still below the $25,000 target, so the Twist's qualitative finding (the 'clean' pick no longer clears the target once revenue risk is priced in) is stable across the full flex range. This does not change margin_pct, which is computed on the untwisted base metric.
